html:
SMTO-POL-0023 — SMTO blocked a command that could seriously damage a computer

GUID: 14cc88b1-c9d1-46fb-a228-68a4e7b174a2
Slug: shell-destructive-policy-denied
Domain: POL · Subsystem: pol

What happened

  • The command would shut down or restart a computer, wipe a disk or delete from the top of a drive, or it hid such an action inside a script SMTO couldn't check. SMTO blocked it before it ran.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Reply telling the Agent exactly what should change, for example 'delete only the files in the old-logs folder', instead of a broad cleanup. Commands that format disks or delete from the top of a drive are always refused, but narrow ones can be checked.
  2. If you didn't mean to restart, shut down or erase anything, ask the Agent to rewrite the step so it doesn't include shutdown, reboot, mkfs or dd at all. SMTO refuses scripts that mention these, even harmlessly, because it can't tell whether they would run.
  3. If you really need to restart or shut down a computer, ask the Agent to run that one command by itself, not inside a script or a chain of commands. SMTO can then see exactly what the command does and may ask for your approval instead of blocking it. If it is still blocked, do it yourself on that computer.

What success looks like

  • The revised command runs and makes only the narrow change you asked for.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't send the same command again with sudo or a different approval; it will be blocked the same way.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Command inspection found a hard-blocked destructive form (shutdown, reboot, mkfs, rm with flags on the root path, dd with if= or of=) that was not recognized as an owner-authorizable action, or such code inside a code-bearing argument or opaque shell syntax, so the command was denied before execution.

What this means

  • Deterministic command inspection found a blocked destructive form or executable content whose destructive scope could not be safely separated from data. Policy and approval decisions are scoped to their owning operation. Existing receipts determine prior effects; this explanation neither grants authority nor changes retry ownership.

Why this can happen

  • Deterministic command inspection found a blocked destructive form or executable content whose destructive scope could not be safely separated from data.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the exact rejected command construct and intended resource scope; distinguish recognized supported owner-authorized operations from opaque embedded code.

How to fix it

  • Read the denial text to see which pattern matched (execution/native_safety.py shell_destructive_reason). Rewrite the operation with an explicit narrow scope and without destructive constructs embedded in code arguments (bash -c, python -c, eval) or opaque syntax; elevation and approval cannot override this denial, but a standalone, structurally parsed host-control or block-device command is routed to the owner-authorizable unsafe-action flow instead.
  • Change the operation to a supported scoped action. Privilege elevation and approval cannot override this deterministic denial.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • A supported explicitly scoped operation satisfies the same safety check under its actual authority.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • Policy and approval decisions are scoped to their owning operation. Existing receipts determine prior effects; this explanation neither grants authority nor changes retry ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
